gap_proposals.description: Sources require guardians to see where a child's bus is and forbid buying hardware or touching engine systems, but they do not say how location is obtained, at what frequency, or from which device or service.

A heads-up before the bus reaches the guardian's stop is required, but lead time, trigger (distance vs ETA vs geofence), channel, and message content are unspecified and could be implemented in materially different ways.
'More than about ten minutes behind' is approximate. The baseline (schedule, typical arrival, last stop), measurement method, and whether the threshold is exact or flexible are not defined.

Guardians may see only their own child's assigned bus, but sources do not describe identity proofing, child-to-guardian-to-bus assignment data, stop association, or how assignment changes are handled.
'The school office should know' does not specify which office (each school vs transportation), recipient roles, channel, or whether the alert is per route, per school, or district-wide.

Tablets are cited as already issued so hardware will not be bought; it is not stated that those tablets will (or can) provide location. Treating them as the tracking platform is an unsupported but material assumption.
Approaching-stop heads-ups, own-bus-only visibility, and lateness relative to a stop all depend on route, stop, assignment, and schedule data that are not identified as available.

Fleet context is 41 buses, 6300 students, and 22 schools, but initial rollout is two high-school routes. Boundaries for driver software, admin tools, remaining routes, elementary/middle schools, and after-September expansion are unclear.

Desired outcomes (guardian location visibility, approaching-stop heads-up, late-bus office notice, phased September start) have no measurable success conditions such as location accuracy, notification lead time, delivery rate, or privacy-incident rate.
The settled rule that guardians never see the whole fleet has no stated test, audit, or proof obligation that isolation holds under mis-assignment, sharing, or client tampering.
Approaching-stop heads-ups and the ~10-minute late office notice lack an explicit way to prove they fire at the intended threshold and only then.

Live bus location for a child's route is a material privacy and safety exposure. The only stated control is hiding the rest of the fleet; retention, sharing, authentication, and unauthorized access are not addressed.
Rollout starts with two high-school routes in September, but calendar year, exact dates, route identifiers, and readiness criteria are absent.

Evidence supports only an initial two high-school-route start and a one-route-at-a-time pattern. There is not enough information to conclude scope, order, or timing for the remaining routes or schools.

The superintendent is explicit and settled only on own-bus-only visibility. Remaining product, privacy, rollout, and operational decisions are stated by the transport director with no visible authority resolving them.

semantic_proposals.mission: Give guardians live visibility of only the bus assigned to their child and a heads-up before that bus reaches their stop, and notify the school office when a bus is running more than about ten minutes behind, using existing driver tablets and guardian phones without new hardware, engine-system changes, or attendance features.

semantic_proposals.statement: Guardians should be able to see where their child's bus is.
Guardians should get a heads-up before the bus reaches their stop.
If a bus is running more than about ten minutes behind, the school office should know.
Roll out one route at a time, starting with the two high-school routes in September.
Guardians receive location and approaching-stop information for their child's assigned bus on their own phones.
The school office becomes aware when a bus is more than about ten minutes behind.
Guardians must only ever see the bus assigned to their own child and must never see the whole fleet.
The district is not buying hardware for this effort.
The solution must not touch the buses' engine systems in any way.
Attendance is not part of this solution and the schools' existing attendance system must not be replaced.
If a bus is running more than about ten minutes behind, the school office must be informed.
Rollout must proceed one route at a time, beginning with the two high-school routes in September.
Drivers already carry district-issued Android tablets with a data plan; that existing device context is the available onboard hardware.
Guardians use their own phones.
The superintendent's rule that guardians never see the whole fleet is settled and must not be reopened.
Buying hardware is out of scope.
Interacting with buses' engine systems is out of scope.
Attendance tracking and replacing the schools' attendance system are out of scope.
Showing guardians the whole fleet is out of scope.
The district runs forty-one buses covering six thousand three hundred students across twenty-two schools.
Drivers already carry district-issued Android tablets with a data plan.
The schools have their own attendance system.

Existing district-issued Android tablets and their data plans will be used as the onboard means to support bus location visibility, because no hardware will be purchased and engine systems will not be touched.
A usable mapping from each child to an assigned bus and stop exists or will be available so guardian visibility can be limited to that bus.
A reference schedule or expected timing exists against which a bus can be judged more than about ten minutes behind.
Guardians have phones capable of receiving the location and heads-up information.

semantic_proposals.prompt: How will bus location be obtained without buying hardware and without touching engine systems?
What timing, channel, and content constitute a guardian heads-up before the bus reaches their stop?
How is more than about ten minutes behind measured, and how is which school office notified?
How are guardians authenticated and bound to only their own child's assigned bus?

semantic_proposals.question: Are the existing district-issued Android tablets intended and capable (GPS, installable software, always-on data) to provide live bus location?
